body.why: Warrior / fighter: the anatomy's sliders are searched inside these

bearing.label: commanding
notes: Chest open and the shoulders settled down and back: armour is carried from the hips, not hunched under.
Weight low and centred over the hips (koshi), knees soft, so the body can move off either foot.
Chin level, gaze to the horizon: enzan no metsuke, "looking at the far mountain", as kendo teaches it.

arms.label: Uchigatana (katana)
notes: uchigatana saya 0.642 m from the art is outside the record (0.66–0.84 m): held at 0.660
uchigatana saya 0.66 m cannot hold a 0.7 m blade: lengthened to 0.735 m

construction.section: shinogi-zukuri: edge (ha), flat (hira-ji) up to the ridge line (shinogi), then the shinogi-ji to the back (mune), iori-mune (peaked)
construction.curve: koshi-zori or torii-zori: the edge on the outside of the curve, deepest just below the middle
construction.hi: often a bo-hi groove along the shinogi-ji, lightening the blade
construction.hamon: midare (irregular) or notare (wavy) in the period; the art decides
construction.tsuka: wood core in ray skin, menuki ornaments under the wrap, bamboo mekugi peg through the tang, fuchi collar and kashira cap
construction.wrap: hishi-maki: two flat braids crossing over and under, folded paper hishigami under each crossing make the diamonds (about 7–9 a side)

fittings.label: Habaki
fittings.note: blade collar: holds the sword in the saya by friction at the koiguchi

fittings.label: Seppa
fittings.note: a washer either side of the tsuba

fittings.label: Tsuba
fittings.note: the guard; balances the blade and stops the hand

fittings.label: Fuchi
fittings.note: collar at the guard end of the hilt

fittings.label: Kashira
fittings.note: pommel cap; the wrap passes through its shitodome

fittings.label: Menuki
fittings.note: ornaments under the wrap, one each side, filling the palm

fittings.label: Mekugi
fittings.note: bamboo peg through tsuka and tang

fittings.label: Kurikata
fittings.note: knob on the omote side of the saya for the sageo, a hand below the mouth

fittings.label: Sageo
fittings.note: flat silk cord through the kurikata; tied to the obi or hakama himo

steel.surface: tamahagane, polished to a mirror ji; the hamon a frosted white band of nioi and nie along the edge; the hada grain like wood showing through the polish

hamon.surface: the hardened edge: crystalline, misty, frosted by the polish; milky white against the dark mirror of the ji

same.surface: ray skin: a field of small hard nodules, ivory-white, showing through the diamonds of the wrap

ito.surface: flat braided silk, wrapped in crossing turns over hishigami paper folds

fittings.surface: gilt copper or shakudō: fuchi, kashira, menuki and habaki

tsuba.surface: forged iron, dark patina, a raised rim (mimi) and relief or openwork

seppa.surface: copper washers either side of the tsuba

saya.surface: honoki (magnolia) wood under many coats of urushi lacquer, deep and glassy

horn.surface: buffalo horn: koiguchi, kurikata and kojiri

carry.how: thrust through the obi (over armour, the uwa-obi), hilt forward
carry.tie: the sageo wraps the saya below the kurikata and its ends tie off at the obi

behaviour.scabbard: Rigid. Pinned where it passes through the obi: it turns with the hips, not the legs, and the kojiri trails, rising when the hips rotate and the stride opens.
behaviour.cord: The sageo's free ends hang and swing with every step; they are cloth on the move, not part of the saya.
behaviour.draw: Left hand at the koiguchi, thumb pushes the tsuba to free the habaki (koiguchi o kiru); the saya is drawn back (saya-biki) as the blade leaves, edge-up, straight into the first cut (nukitsuke).
behaviour.sheathe: Noto: the blade's back slides across the left hand to the koiguchi, tip in, the saya pushed forward to meet it.

sources: Morihiro Ogawa, Art of the Samurai (Met, 2009)

arms.label: Wakizashi
arms.why: the flat-lay has it; the turnaround does not wear it
notes: wakizashi is laid out sheathed: its hilt measured against the scabbard; the blade's features are not seen
wakizashi tsuka 0.313 m from the art is outside the record (0.14–0.2 m): held at 0.200

construction.hamon: matches the katana when made as a pair

steel.surface: tamahagane, polished to a mirror ji; the hamon a frosted white band of nioi and nie along the edge; the hada grain like wood showing through the polish

seppa.surface: copper washers either side of the tsuba

saya.surface: honoki (magnolia) wood under many coats of urushi lacquer, deep and glassy

horn.surface: buffalo horn: koiguchi, kurikata and kojiri

carry.how: thrust through the obi inside the katana

behaviour.scabbard: Rigid, rides the obi closer to the body than the katana.

companions.note: A samurai of the period carried a shorter companion blade with the uchigatana; the pairing became the formal daishō in the Edo period.
Every saya has its sageo, a flat braided silk cord through the kurikata, tied to the obi or hakama himo so the scabbard cannot slip out on the draw.

wear: Over armour the swords are thrust through the uwa-obi, an outer sash tied over the dō (tosei-gusoku); without armour, through the obi over the kosode.
Uchigatana edge-up at the left hip, hilt forward and across the belly, the saya angled down and back past the hip.
The wakizashi rides inside the katana, closer to the body, at a steeper angle.
The tachi, older and for mounted warriors, hangs edge-down from the belt on two hangers (ashi): never confuse the two.

atlas.name: Kendo
atlas.lede: Behind the mask and armour, kendo preserves the samurai’s swordsmanship as a thunderous modern discipline where a single perfect cut — spirit, sword and body as one — decides everything.
atlas.technique: Kendoka strike four targets — men (head), kote (wrist), do (trunk) and tsuki (throat thrust) — with the shinai, gripped for cutting rather than hitting.

atlas.name: Judo
atlas.lede: From a small temple hall in Tokyo, an educator distilled the samurai’s jujutsu into a modern path of maximum efficiency — and built the first Asian martial art to conquer the Olympic Games.
atlas.technique: Judo’s core is the throw: te-waza (hand), koshi-waza (hip) and ashi-waza (foot) techniques, all premised on kuzushi — breaking the opponent’s balance before applying leverage.

atlas.name: Sumo
atlas.era: ancient ritual roots — Edo-period professional tournaments
atlas.lede: Half sacred rite, half explosive collision of giants, sumo compresses centuries of Shinto ceremony into bouts that can end in seconds on a ring of consecrated clay.
atlas.technique: Bouts begin with the tachiai, a synchronized explosive charge; victory comes by forcing the opponent out of the 4.55-metre dohyo or making any part of his body beyond the soles touch the ground.

sources: Kōkan Nagayama, The Connoisseur's Book of Japanese Swords (Kodansha, 1997)
Thomas D. Conlan, Weapons and Fighting Techniques of the Samurai Warrior 1200–1877 (Amber, 2008)
Morihiro Ogawa, Art of the Samurai: Japanese Arms and Armor, 1156–1868 (The Metropolitan Museum of Art, 2009)
